question: Can large multimodal models infer an unfamiliar physical law from demonstrations and then apply it to synthetic collision videos, rather than merely recalling ordinary physics or exploiting language cues?

key_findings.claim: InPhyRe explicitly separates ordinary collision laws from irregular worlds that violate one or more familiar conservation relationships.
key_findings.evidence: The generator controls object trajectories and constructs question-answer episodes under regular and deliberately modified rules, allowing the same models to be tested on recall-compatible physics and on induction from demonstrations.

key_findings.claim: Thirteen evaluated multimodal models perform markedly worse on irregular scenarios, even when demonstrations state or exhibit the operative rule.
key_findings.evidence: Across model sizes and prompt variants, accuracy falls substantially between regular and irregular splits. Extra examples and chain-of-thought help some settings but do not remove the gap, and their marginal benefit diminishes.

key_findings.claim: A language-bias audit suggests that many apparent in-context gains do not depend strongly on the demonstration video itself.
key_findings.evidence: Video-only demonstrations sharply lower performance, while replacing a demonstration video with a random or mismatched one changes accuracy by less than one percentage point for 86.8 percent of tested model-condition combinations. This points to textual templates and priors carrying much of the signal.

key_findings.claim: The benchmark diagnoses a mixture of perception, rule induction, and answer grounding rather than isolating pure physical reasoning.
key_findings.evidence: The authors' error analyses show that models can verbalize conservation principles yet hallucinate scene conditions or apply them inconsistently. They also acknowledge that simple renderings limit perceptual realism and that more complex controllable generated video remains an open construction problem.

method.core_idea: Generate paired regular and counterfactual physical worlds so that success on the latter requires inferring a local rule from multimodal demonstrations instead of relying on memorized textbook laws.
method.mechanism: A procedural simulator produces collision videos and questions under controlled conservation or violation rules. Models receive demonstrations and answer queries under zero-shot, in-context, chain-of-thought, fine-tuned, and modality-ablation conditions; mismatched-video interventions probe which part of a demonstration they use.
assumptions: Procedurally rendered collisions are perceptually clear enough that low accuracy primarily reflects reasoning rather than object-tracking failure.
Irregular rules are expressible and inferable from the supplied number and diversity of demonstrations.
Answer accuracy and perturbation tests are adequate proxies for internal rule induction.
The selected collision-rule family represents inductive physical reasoning beyond this generator.

techniques.role: Creates worlds that systematically violate familiar physical relationships.
Separates use of parametric physics knowledge from induction of a demonstrated rule.
Tests whether video-text examples teach the rule needed for a new query.
Audits whether model answers causally depend on demonstration visual content.

evaluations.setting: Regular and irregular collision scenarios evaluated on 13 large multimodal models.
evaluations.metric: Exact or task-specific answer accuracy and the regular-to-irregular accuracy gap.
evaluations.result: Most models retain a large negative gap on irregular rules; stronger general performance does not imply robust induction.
evaluations.baseline: The same model and prompt on regular, familiar-physics scenarios.

evaluations.setting: Increasing numbers and variants of in-context demonstrations, with chain-of-thought and fine-tuning controls.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy gain over zero-shot and residual irregular-split gap.
evaluations.result: Demonstrations improve selected models but gains saturate and do not consistently close the regular-irregular difference.
evaluations.baseline: Zero-shot prompting, direct-answer prompting, and regular-world performance.

evaluations.setting: Video-only, text-only, random-video, and mismatched-video demonstration interventions.
evaluations.metric: Change in answer accuracy after removing or corrupting one modality.
evaluations.result: Video-only performance drops sharply, whereas most video swaps change accuracy by under one point, indicating weak use of visual evidence in the demonstrations.

limitations: Synthetic scenes are visually simple and do not span the perceptual complexity of real physical systems.
The benchmark's collision laws cover a bounded family of counterfactuals and may reward template learning.
Accuracy cannot by itself distinguish failed perception, failed induction, and failed answer execution.
Fine-tuning and prompting results depend on model-specific interfaces and finite evaluation budgets.
failure_modes: A model may infer answers from linguistic regularities while ignoring the demonstration video.
Memorized conservation laws can override a clearly demonstrated counterfactual law.
Tracking or numeric-extraction errors can masquerade as reasoning failures.
Repeated templates may permit shortcut classification without a transferable world model.
reusable_insights: Counterfactual rules are a useful control for separating recall of scientific facts from induction.
Randomized or mismatched modality interventions reveal whether multimodal demonstrations are used causally.
Benchmark reports should decompose perception, rule identification, and application rather than label their aggregate as reasoning.
open_questions: How can realistic video generators vary physical laws while preserving exact ground truth and avoiding artifacts?
Would interactive experimentation, rather than passive demonstrations, materially improve rule discovery?
Which process-level probes can tell genuine latent rule induction from prompt-template matching?

competitive_landscape.title: PHYRE: A New Benchmark for Physical Reasoning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Uses procedurally generated physical scenes to test action-conditioned reasoning and cross-task generalization.
competitive_landscape.difference: PHYRE evaluates planning under ordinary simulator dynamics; InPhyRe focuses on inferring counterfactual laws from demonstrations with multimodal language models.

competitive_landscape.title: Physion: Evaluating Physical Prediction from Vision in Humans and Machines
competitive_landscape.relationship: Benchmarks visual prediction of physical outcomes across controlled scene families.
competitive_landscape.difference: Physion tests prediction under stable real-world-like dynamics and human comparison; InPhyRe changes the law itself and tests in-context induction.

competitive_landscape.title: IntPhys 2: Benchmarking Intuitive Physics Understanding in Multimodal Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Evaluates contemporary multimodal models on broad intuitive-physics video questions.
competitive_landscape.difference: IntPhys 2 emphasizes coverage of ordinary intuitive physics; InPhyRe's paired irregular worlds are designed to invalidate memorized priors and expose induction failures.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: InPhyRe is a controlled benchmark for inductive physical reasoning in which a model must discover and apply unfamiliar physical laws.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The regular/irregular pairing and modality-mismatch experiments directly test behavior that ordinary intuitive-physics datasets confound with stored knowledge.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest contribution is not another collision dataset but the counterfactual-law control plus causal audit of demonstration modalities; claims of pure reasoning failure should remain qualified by perceptual and template confounds.
